column3: Its question about being a guardian over one ruled by desire parallels the limit placed on the addressee, but not rescue from punishment.
The divine names do not clarify the due punishment-word or the rescue question.
Being turned away from truth is a broad antecedent to judgment, not an account of the punishment-word or rescue.
It explicitly says that punishment has become due upon many, then denies that one disgraced by God has an honoring rescuer.
The immediately preceding verse sets those guided by hearing and following the best speech against the person whose punishment has become due.
It repeats the formula of the Lord's word becoming due upon persistent transgressors and explains it through their settled unbelief.
Its rhetorical question denies the messenger power to compel belief, closely paralleling the limit on rescuing one under judgment.
Abandoning received signs and being pursued into error gives a plausible path toward the settled state in the focus, without its judgment formula.
It exactly joins the Lord's word becoming due upon disbelievers with their being companions of the Fire.
The creation comparison does not develop the punishment-word or inability to rescue.
Its contrast between fearful worship and heedless equality supplies nearby moral context, but does not state the focus's final judgment.
The prior divine word securing the messengers is a broad counterpart to a word of punishment, not an explanation of its becoming due.
The same surah portrays a person trying to shield his face from the evil punishment, directly developing the Fire-bound consequence.
God's rescue from the brink of a fiery pit supplies the direct positive counterpart to the focus's question about rescue from the Fire.
It depicts God's enemies being gathered toward the Fire, supplying the destination but not the due word or rescue limit.
The rhetorical question about guiding the blind directly parallels the addressee's lack of power to save one in the Fire.
It states that the overwhelmed receive neither a cry for help nor rescue, a parallel limit on deliverance in a different scene.
The jinn's creation from fire does not clarify judgment, culpability, or rescue.
It repeats the rhetorical limit: the addressee cannot make the deaf hear or guide the blind in manifest error.
Temporary mercy and enjoyment do not materially clarify the due punishment or rescue question.
Those invoked besides God cannot recover even what a fly takes, providing a limited analogy for powerless rescue.
The question whether the addressee can make the deaf hear closely parallels the denied capacity to rescue the condemned.
Following Pharaoh's unsound command gives a broad account of misguiding leadership, not the focus's judgment or rescue question.
Its condemnation of a false utterance does not establish the punishment-word or rescue from the Fire.
Those already in the Fire ask its keepers for even one day's reduction of punishment, underscoring their inability to escape it.
Failure to appraise God rightly is a general background for wrongdoing but does not develop the focus's sequence.
It links disbelief in meaningful creation to the Fire, a consequential parallel without the focus's formula or rescue question.
It repeats that the word has become due upon them and places the people within a continuing class of losers.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire, adding a concrete route into the destination but not the focus's limit on rescue.
The command to protect oneself and family from the Fire presents prevention before the condition in which rescue is denied.
It restates the exact punishment-word formula at the gates of Hell after the disbelievers acknowledge the messengers' warnings.
The sign of a laden ship does not clarify punishment becoming due or rescue from the Fire.
Fire is sent against jinn and humans and they cannot defend themselves, a related picture of powerless exposure.
A prior word from the Lord and an appointed term explain why an otherwise binding consequence is delayed.
Following the revealed way rather than ignorant desires provides a moral alternative to the settled condition described in the focus.
Creation in truth and return to God provide only a broad horizon for the verse's final judgment.
God's aid to the messenger and the lowering of the disbelievers' word only loosely contrast with the focus's unrescuable punishment.
It portrays desire-led error, sealed hearing and heart, veiled sight, and asks who could guide such a person after God.
The assertion that none can alter God's words supports the firmness of divine decree, though the verse concerns aid to messengers.
The same surah contrasts a breast opened to Islam with hardened hearts in manifest error, illuminating the moral state before 39:19.
It exactly says that those upon whom the Lord's word has become due will not believe.
Its use of haqq concerns the speakers' claimed entitlement, not a divinely due word of punishment.
The denied Fire is presented directly to its deniers, showing punishment becoming an unavoidable experienced reality.
It contrasts being cast into the Fire with arriving secure on the Day, but does not explain why the sentence became due.
The true Day and the option to take a return to the Lord mark the decision before the focus's irreversible condition.
The enduring word left among Abraham's descendants concerns return, offering a thematic but non-identical word-and-response parallel.
It warns of the Fire prepared for disbelievers, supplying the destination without the focus's question of rescue.
Those shown the Fire admit it is true and are told to taste punishment for their disbelief, directly joining truth, Fire, and consequence.
Rejecting truth brings the news they mocked, providing a pattern in which denial is met by the realized consequence.
A question about wonder at the discourse does not materially clarify judgment or rescue.
The command to taste punishment and the Fire's punishment for disbelievers supplies a general consequence parallel.
The word of taqwa attached to believers forms a positive contrast to the word of punishment becoming due upon others.
God establishes truth by His words, a broad counterpart to the focus's effective divine word.
The assigned right in wealth does not clarify the punishment-word or saving from the Fire.
The triumph of the religion of truth is too general to explain the due punishment or the rescue question.
The preserved mention among later generations has no material connection to the focus.
It joins clear evidence and mercy with belief, while assigning the Fire as the appointment for those who disbelieve.
Its fire imagery belongs to a metaphor of truth and falsehood, not the punitive Fire or denied rescue.
The same surah links short-lived enjoyment in disbelief with becoming a companion of the Fire.
The speaker rejects false gods because their intercession cannot avail and they cannot rescue him, directly matching the rescue limitation.
It sets an invitation to salvation against an invitation to the Fire, making the opposed destinations explicit.
The phrase true certainty confirms reality generally but does not add a route to the due punishment-word.
Its legal procedure for disputed testimony does not clarify the focus's judgment or rescue.
The contrast between knowing revealed truth and blindness provides a moral counterpart to the focus's settled unbelief.
The prohibition on repeating a slander does not develop the punishment-word or rescue from the Fire.
It states that Hell already encompasses the disbelievers, directly intensifying the focus's image of one in the Fire.
Bodily testimony on the Day does not materially clarify the due punishment or capacity to rescue.
It declares that one brought into the Fire is disgraced and that wrongdoers have no helpers, directly supporting the absence of rescue.
Neither wealth nor children can avail against God, and the people become abiding companions of the Fire.
It assigns idolaters and their objects of worship as fuel entering Hell, a direct destination parallel without the due-word formula.
It links disbelief and denial of signs with abiding companionship in the Fire, giving the broad condition and outcome.
It calls the dispute of the people of the Fire a certain truth, supporting the reality of the focus's final scene.
The truthful recitation of signs and messenger status do not clarify the punishment-word or rescue limit.
The general threat of the greatest punishment does not specify the focus's due decree or inability to save.
Its Fire-companion statement is retained only as rejected contrast evidence and does not add positive support for the focus reading.
Mercy and the certain gathering provide a broad eschatological frame, but not the focus's punishment or rescue logic.
The question about kindling worldly fire does not develop punitive Fire or rescue.
After universal messengerly warning, it says misguidance became due upon some and directs attention to the end of deniers.
It describes bearing sin and becoming a companion of the Fire as the recompense of wrongdoers.
The word of decision delays final judgment, while wrongdoers remain promised painful punishment, closely illuminating decree and consequence.
The unchangeability of God's words supports their reliability, though this verse concerns good news for God's allies.
It depicts continual exposure to the Fire followed by entry into the severest punishment, concretizing the condition from which rescue is absent.
Those dragged face-down in the Fire are told to taste it, a vivid consequence parallel without the focus's decree formula.
A corrupt foundation collapses with its builders into the fire of Hell, showing a self-incurred descent into the destination.
Its brief statement of entering a scorching Fire adds only the destination.
The jinn's humiliating worldly labor after Solomon's death does not clarify the focus's punishment or rescue.
Testing Abraham with words and denying the covenant to wrongdoers only loosely parallels divine judgment becoming due.
Good words and righteous action rise while plotters face punishment, but the verse does not develop the focus's rescue limit.
Noah's appeal concerning his son shows that a plea cannot redefine the scope of a settled divine judgment.
God stands over every soul and what it earns, supporting individual accountability before the focus's consequence.
Mockery of charitable believers ends in painful punishment, a general wrongdoing-to-punishment relation.
Those who seek to leave the Fire are returned to it and told to taste the punishment they denied, directly ruling out escape.
The believers' communal character and promised reward do not clarify the punishment-word or denied rescue.
A spoken word of disbelief and subsequent turning lead to painful punishment, connecting speech, rejection, and consequence.
Jonah's selection among the righteous does not materially clarify the focus.
God's promise is true, offering a broad statement of the reliability of divine declarations without the punishment sequence.
The question about hastening punishment confirms its anticipated reality but does not address its becoming due or rescue.
God removes falsehood and establishes truth by His words, a broad counterpart to the effectual divine word in the focus.
The hypothetical opening of a heavenly gate does not clarify punishment or rescue from the Fire.
Its command to speak only truth about God and its use of word for Jesus do not develop the punitive word in the focus.
When a town persists in defiance, the word becomes due upon it before its destruction, an exact decree-to-consequence parallel.
Those upon whom the word has become due acknowledge having led others astray, directly pairing the formula with culpable guidance.
It explicitly says the word became due upon them among prior communities after their companions made their deeds seem fair.
The speakers confess that their Lord's word became due upon them and that they must taste its consequence.
God declares that His word has become due to fill Hell with jinn and humankind, directly connecting the fixed word to the Fire.
The completed word of the Lord to fill Hell with jinn and humankind gives the encompassing fulfillment behind the focus's Fire scene.
God's word of truth to fill Hell with Iblis and his followers makes the decree and its destination explicit.
It contrasts the guided group with those upon whom misguidance has become due because they chose false protectors.
Opposing the messenger and following another way leads to being turned toward that choice and burned in Hell.
Those God leaves astray have no protector besides Him and are gathered blind into Hell, where the blaze is repeatedly increased.
The Fire has surrounded the disbelievers and its attempted relief becomes further punishment, directly presenting inescapable enclosure.
Hell displayed openly to the disbelievers supplies the eschatological destination without the focus's decree formula.
Hell is prepared as the lodging for disbelievers, directly supporting the focus's person already in the Fire.
The disbelievers cannot ward the Fire from their faces or backs and will receive no help, closely matching denied rescue.
Being thrown bound into a constricted place in Hell intensifies the image of a person enclosed in the Fire.
Those cursed in Hell will find neither protector nor helper, directly denying any rescuing support.
The people of the Fire neither die nor receive a reduction of its punishment, making their inability to escape explicit.
The same surah names Hell as the abode of the arrogant, extending the focus's immediate judgment setting.
The command to enter Hell's gates and remain there provides the completed outcome after the punishment-word in the same surah.
The people in the Fire dispute among themselves, concretizing the community already subject to the focus's punishment.
The keepers of Hell direct its people back to the rejected messengerly warnings, showing why no reduction or rescue is available.
The people of Hell ask Malik for an end, but are told that they will remain, reinforcing the permanence of their condition.
It assigns those who disbelieve in their Lord the punishment of Hell and calls it an evil destination.
The people of the Blaze admit that hearing or understanding would have kept them from becoming its companions.
The direct divine threat to drive the rejecter into Saqar gives an explicit sentencing-to-Fire parallel.
Hell lies in wait for transgressors as their return, supplying a direct final-destination parallel.
The people in the Fire are shown their deeds and regrets and are expressly denied any exit from it.
Those in the Fire seek to leave it but cannot, directly supporting the focus's denied deliverance.
The Fire is named as the lasting abode of those gathered through chosen association, linking culpable allegiance to enclosure.
Those who deny the signs are assigned the Fire after every avenue of ascent is closed to them.
Every person will approach Hell, described as an unavoidable decree binding upon the Lord.
Whoever comes to the Lord as a criminal has Hell, where one neither dies nor lives.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out and make their future conduct conditional, directly presenting an unsuccessful plea for rescue.
Hell is presented as the reality repeatedly promised to those who disbelieved.
Layers of Fire above and below the disbelievers portray total enclosure and amplify the focus's location in the Fire.
The enemies of God receive the Fire as their abode and recompense for rejecting His signs.
The criminals remain in Hell's punishment without relief, a direct permanence parallel.
Those who forgot the meeting day are forgotten in the Fire and cannot escape it or seek restoration.
A blazing Fire is prepared for those who do not believe in God and His messenger.
The command to cast every stubborn disbeliever into Hell gives a direct judicial transition into the Fire.
Hell is identified as the reality denied by the criminals before they circulate within it and boiling water.
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs are abiding companions of the Fire, a concise condition-and-destination parallel.
The wives of Noah and Lot enter the Fire with its people despite their proximity to righteous servants, illustrating that no human relation rescues.
The unjust become fuel for Hell, directly presenting their final incorporation into the Fire.
Disbelievers who reject the clear proof are abiding in the Fire and are named the worst of creatures.
